metadata.title: Bridging Between Us and Them: Cultivating inclusive attitudes toward immigrants through global citizenship education and intergroup contact in South Korea

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Korea and applies the provided student sampling weight to produce population-representative estimates, consistent with PISA technical-report recommendations. The analytic sample is restricted to 15-year-old students in Korea with non-missing responses on the immigrant-background item used for exclusion and on the key intergroup-contact items (with additional missingness handled via imputation; see missing-data section). The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty quantification is described through multilevel modeling with school-fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors at the school level. Because the analysis is regression-based (not ML training), the paper does not discuss any ML-specific omission of weights; instead it explicitly states that the student weight was applied.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 for Korea and restricted to 15-year-old students in the assessment. In Korea, the survey included 6650 students across 188 schools; six students with immigrant backgrounds and 74 non-respondents on the immigrant-background item were excluded, yielding an analytic sample of 6570. Missing values ranged from 0% (gender) to 3% (intergroup contact); the study retained cases and addressed missingness via multiple imputation (50 imputed datasets pooled).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Korea, 15-year-olds) Inclusive attitudes toward immigrants (IATI) scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel models with school-fixed effects and cluster-robust SEs. Model 1 (main effects): GCE (1) +0.130 SD (p<.01), GCE (2) +0.219 SD (p<.001), GCE (3) +0.250 SD (p<.001), GCE (4) +0.295 SD (p<.001). Model 2 (interactions): Contact in school × GCE (4) +0.272 SD (p<.01); Contact in school main effect −0.182 SD (p<.05) when GCE=0; Contact in community main effect +0.087 SD (p>.05). Controls: SES +0.060 SD (p<.001), Female +0.140 SD (p<.001), Reading newspaper ns, Reading online news +0.046 SD (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Korea, 15-year-olds) the study leveraged GCE exposure (types count), intergroup contact in school, intergroup contact in community, and student background controls to predict inclusive attitudes toward immigrants (IATI), finding that more types of GCE were associated with higher IATI (up to +0.295 SD for four types) and that GCE significantly moderated the school-contact relationship only when students experienced all four GCE types (interaction +0.272 SD, p<.01). This indicates that strengthening comprehensive, multi-component global citizenship education in schools may help students convert intergroup contact into more inclusive attitudes toward immigrants, though the evidence is correlational due to the cross-sectional design.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for Korea (15-year-olds; analytic sample N=6570 across 188 schools) to examine whether global citizenship education (GCE) fosters inclusive attitudes toward immigrants (IATI) and whether it moderates intergroup contact in school and community. IATI is measured as a Likert-based composite scale (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.89), while GCE exposure is operationalized as four binary items summed into dummy variables for exposure to 1–4 types. Using multilevel regression with school-fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors, the authors report that GCE shows positive, non-linear associations with IATI (+0.130 to +0.295 SD across 1–4 types, all significant), and that the interaction between school contact and GCE is significant only for students exposed to all four GCE types (+0.272 SD, p<.01). Intergroup contact in the community is not significantly associated with IATI, and no significant community-contact interactions emerge. Missing data are handled via multiple imputation (50 datasets pooled), but the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
